# `p256` — recorded 2026-09-12

| | |
|---|---|
| **Job** | The curve under ES256. `docs/PHASE-2-ADMIN-AND-AUDIT-DESIGN.md` §15.3 chose ES256 for all three signing roles — grant signatures (§3.3), the browser session key (§4.2) and the organisation root key (§6.1) — and this crate is NIST P-256 with the ECDSA glue for it |
| **Version** | `0.14.0`, `default-features = false`, `features = ["ecdsa"]` |
| **Publisher** | RustCrypto — by repository URL (`https://github.com/RustCrypto/elliptic-curves`). `deps/decisions/00-CLOSURE-SERVER.md`'s caveat applies verbatim: a repository URL is written by the crate's author and proves nothing about who holds the publish token |
| **Licence** | Apache-2.0 OR MIT — compatible with ADR-0004 |
| **Ships or tooling** | **Ships.** Linked into `fathom-server` |
| **`build.rs`** | None — no `build.rs` in the published tree (`~/.cargo/registry/src/.../p256-0.14.0/`, listed 2026-09-12) |
| **Proc macros** | None |
| **Determinism** | Signing is deterministic: `SigningKey`'s `Signer`/`PrehashSigner` impls in `ecdsa 0.17.0` route to `sign_prehashed_rfc6979`, so the same key and the same message give the same signature on every machine. Read out of `ecdsa-0.17.0/src/signing.rs` rather than assumed, because `crates/fathom-server/tests/authority_vectors.rs` pins a signature as a hex literal and that test is only meaningful if the value cannot move. Verification is a pure function of (key, message, signature) |

## Why ES256 and not EdDSA

§15.3's reasoning, unchanged and not re-opened here: **EdDSA was the better primitive on paper and
ten crates cheaper, and it was rejected because FIDO's metadata service was unreachable**, so which
authenticators support EdDSA could not be established. Choosing it would have meant betting on an
unverified belief, which CLAUDE.md rule 1 forbids. ES256 is the choice that does not need the
lookup that could not be done. **Revisit if that service becomes reachable** — the decision is
recorded as contingent, not as a preference.

## Why not first-party

`32` §15 forbids hand-rolling cryptography, and elliptic-curve arithmetic is the least forgiving
place in this project to break that rule. A wrong field reduction, a non-constant-time scalar
multiply or a missing point-on-curve check produces a signature scheme that verifies things it
should not, silently. The rule ADR-0043's vault work already follows applies unchanged.

## What the feature list buys and what it deliberately leaves out

`default-features = false` drops `std`, `pem`, `pkcs8` and `precomputed-tables`. `ecdsa` is the one
feature named; it expands to `arithmetic` (the field and group operations), `ecdsa-core/algorithm`
(the signing half) and `sha256` — the hash in ES256's name, which resolves to the `sha2 0.11.0`
this workspace already names rather than adding one.

`pem` and `pkcs8` are absent on purpose: they are key-**encoding** surface, and the only public keys
this server handles arrive as SEC1 uncompressed points in a `bytea` column whose length is checked
by the database. A PEM parser on the enrolment path would be attacker-supplied input parsed by a
crate nothing else needs.

## Constant time — the claim that must not be overstated

§15.3: *"constant-time is barely relevant to the server here and the design must not claim it is.
The server only verifies; there is no secret scalar in this process on this path."* That is true of
the authority layer as built: `src/authority.rs` verifies with `VerifyingKey`, and the only place a
private key exists in this process is a **test** signing key and the software organisation root key
of §6.1, which §15.1 admits as a deliberate downgrade from hardware. Where it starts to matter is
browser-side key handling, which this crate is not doing yet. No constant-time property is claimed
in this record beyond what the crate's own documentation states.

## Advisories — two databases, both with working controls, 2026-09-12

- **RustSec**, via `cargo audit --file Cargo.lock` (1,243 advisories loaded): 0 vulnerabilities,
  0 warnings across 158 crates. `cargo deny --locked check`: `advisories ok, bans ok, licenses ok,
  sources ok`.
- **OSV.dev**, the aggregate that carries GitHub-reviewed advisories RustSec never receives —
  `docs/PHASE-2-STORAGE-DESIGN.md` §12.5's gap. **`scripts/osv-gate.sh` could not run here: its
  `api.osv.dev/v1/querybatch` endpoint is refused by this session's proxy (`Tunnel connection
  failed: 403 Forbidden`), and the gate fails closed, as designed.** The same database was read
  through the door that is open — the `crates.io` bulk export
  (`osv-vulnerabilities.storage.googleapis.com/crates.io/all.zip`, 2,819 advisories over 1,790
  packages, fetched 2026-09-12) — and checked version-aware against the whole lockfile with a
  positive control (`tokio 1.8.0` must report affected, and does). **Nothing found for `p256`
  at any version, and nothing found against any pinned version in this lockfile.**

That is a result, not a clean bill of health, and it goes stale immediately. **Re-run
`scripts/osv-gate.sh` itself somewhere its endpoint is reachable before merge** — a bulk export
read by hand is not the gate, it is the lookup the gate automates.

## What was NOT established

**The COSE algorithm identifier for ES256 could not be read.** `www.iana.org` returns 403 through
this session's proxy, so the COSE Algorithms registry was not opened, and §3.2's `alg smallint --
COSE algorithm id` is therefore **not** filled with a COSE number by this build. `0011`'s
`account_keys.alg` carries Fathom's own id `1` and a `CHECK` that admits nothing else; whoever
lands WebAuthn either establishes the COSE value and migrates the column, or keeps a Fathom id and
maps at the boundary. Writing a remembered number into a stored column would have been exactly the
confident guess ADR-0034 forbids.
